title: Biodiversity and Conservation of Horticultural Crops
authors: Garima Maurya, Hemant Kumar Singh, Jitendra Kumar, Niharika Bhatnagar, Pathan Maha Jabeen, Shubham Patel
affiliations: Department of Plant Pathology; Acharya Narendra Deva University of Agriculture and Technology,

blocks.x: ABSTRACT

Biodiversity is the key to drive the whole ecosystem as it includes the variety of flora, fauna and microorganisms which form the chain of all biological cycles occurring on the earth. India with its unique and rich agricultural heritage leads to harmonizing horticultural biodiversity and ecological preservation. The dependence on the technological advancements, fostering the education and developing supportive policies with funding framework are very essential strategies. These efforts multiply agricultural outputs but also conserve biodiversity and increase food security and ecosystem flexibility. There are some spot where the diversity is rich and they are called ‘hotspots’ which includes variety of vascular plants found nowhere else. Owing to civilization, these hotspots are under severe threat, having losses over 70% of their original vegetation. The recorded decline across successive years has been mostly ascribed to habitat degradation and fragmentation, the proliferation of invasive alien species, consequences of global warming, various forms of environmental pollution, and the occurrence of natural disasters. Hence, keeping in mind the closeness of biodiversity with human it needs to be protected. Biodiversity conservation assembles the methods of protecting, managing and restoring the biodiversity. It utilizes two main strategies which are in-situ and ex-situ conservation, in-situ includes national parks, wildlife centuries, biosphere reserves while ex-situ includes zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks and gene banks. The Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), adopted during the Rio Earth Summit in 1992, explicitly advocates this principle and emphasizes the formulation of strategies aimed at conserving biological diversity while ensuring its sustainable utilization. Keywords-climate change; convention; hotspots; microorganisms; strategies
INTRODUCTION:

The biosphere encompasses an immense range of diversity that extends beyond the species level, permeating all hierarchies of biological organization from complex macromolecular assemblies within cells to the vast ecological structures represented by biomes. Ecologically, biodiversity is the key to drive all the biological cycles occurring on the earth that recycle vital parts like carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, sulphur, and water between living and non-living components of the atmosphere. Biologists commonly conceptualize biodiversity as the comprehensive sum of genetic resources, species richness, and ecosystem variability within a particular region (Sahane et al., 2010). Biodiversity, a term popularized by sociobiologist Edward O. Wilson, is defined as the integrated diversity across all levels of biological organization encompassing genes, species, and ecosystems while simultaneously highlighting its relevance to human welfare, cultural values, and sustainable development. India is one of the 17 megadiverse countries, occupying 2.4% of the earth’s land area which harbours the important species of flora, fauna and microorganisms.

Horticulture, as a notable component of agriculture, plays a vital role in India's wealth and food security. Its role extends beyond the fields and orchards into urban development and landscaping, contributing to the rejuvenation of cities, boosting urban biodiversity, and improving the quality of life. The sector has been involved in India's agricultural success, contributing to crop diversity, nutritional security, and providing employment of to weaker sections of society. Horticultural crops provide twice as number of jobs as compared to traditional cereal crops. As a consequence of sustained growth, India has established itself as the world’s second-largest producer of fruits and vegetables, while continuing to maintain a dominant position in the cultivation of spices, coconut, and cashew nut. By August 2025, during the 2024-25 period, the nation’s horticultural output had risen markedly from 280.70 million tonnes in 2013-14 to 367.72 million tonnes. This expansion comprised 114.51 million tonnes of fruits, 219.67 million tonnes of vegetables, and 33.54 million tonnes derived from other horticultural crops, underscoring both the scale and diversity of India’s agricultural sector. The practices of horticulture ranging from traditional to modern technological methods, have profound implications for the conservation and enhancement of biodiversity. But, today’s fast-growing world on one hand have potential to support the horticultural biodiversity by implementing various technological and genetic tools on other hand, the intensive agricultural practices can affect the biodiversity through soil degradation, water extraction, habitat loss, excess use of chemical fertilizers and high energy consumption. Horticultural crops constitute an essential component of the Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture (PGRFA), representing a wide spectrum of species and remarkable diversity. Crop genetic variation plays a critical role in sustaining production levels and ensuring nutritional security across diverse agro-ecological regions. Equally vital is the diversity of soil microorganisms, which underpin ecosystem health by disintegrate organic matter, recycling nutrients, and facilitating nitrogen transformations. On-farm practices such as crop rotations, species mixtures, permanent soil cover in conservation agriculture, and agroforestry systems further enhance yield stability and soil fertility, thereby supporting both ecological resilience and human livelihoods. This immense wealth of biodiversity has evolved over millions of years of evolution, yet current rates of species loss threaten to erode it within less than two centuries. The implicit outcomes for humanity are profound, as biodiversity underpins food security, cultural heritage, and ecological balance. Recognizing this, biodiversity conservation has become an acute planetary threat, with increasing awareness that safeguarding biological diversity is indispensable for human survival, well-being, and sustainable development.
TYPES OF HORTICULTURAL BIODIVERSITY:

Horticulture encompasses the cultivation of a wide array of plants for food, medicinal purposes, and beautification. Its role extends beyond the fields and orchards into urban development and landscaping, contributing to the greening of cities, enhancing urban biodiversity, and improving the quality of life for city dwellers. On one hand, Horticultural practices can play a major role in enhancing biodiversity by sustaining diverse plant species, providing habitats, and preserving genetic variation within crops. On the other, intensive horticultural practices disrupts ecological balance through habitat destruction, the use of chemical pesticides and fertilizers, water extraction, and the introduction of invasive species.

The exception is to bring more fruits and vegetables, and replicate it viably. A legitimate production along with ecosystem avenue is incumbent to veil with degrading environment and uncertainties as a result of climate change. The major intent is to assist the income generating farmers so that we can add value to products, higher returns can be generated for producers, while simultaneously promoting collaboration between the public and private sectors.
Horticultural biodiversity is very diverse and it includes the following types (Campbell, 2003): Genetic diversity,
Species diversity,
Ecosystem diversity

Genetic diversity: A single species can display extensive genetic diversity across its full geographical distribution. The sources of genetic diversity occur in nature in various forms like land races, wild relatives, mutations, hybridization and germplasm collections. The productivity of horticultural crops is closely tied to the strategic use of genetic resources, enabling the evolution of uniform, high-quality produce that can oppose shifting environmental conditions while meeting evolving market expectations. Beyond technical efficiency, this optimization supports farmers’ livelihoods, strengthens food security, and secure that agricultural systems endure resilient and responsive to human needs in a changing world. Brassica oleracea species is a remarkable example of high genetic diversity, as breeding over 2500 years has produced a wide range of distinct vegetables (cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kale, kohlrabi, brussels sprouts) from a single wild ancestor. India possesses an extraordinary wealth of plant genetic resources, with more than 50,000 distinct strains of rice and around 1,000 varieties of mango, including the renowned Dashehari, Alphonso, Langra. There is interspecific variation between species of citrus (orange, lemon, lime). A very high variability is present in solanaceous vegetables (tomato, brinjal, chilli), cucurbits (ridge gourd, pointed gourd, cucumber), and tuber crops (taro, yams). The North- Eastern region of India is a hotspot, containing numerous wild fruit species and relatives of cultivated crops. The genetic erosion is being recorded in horticultural crops due to replacement of traditional varieties by modern hybrids, monoculture practices, urbanization and habitat destruction. Species diversity: The diversity of horticultural crops at the species level is much different in various agro-ecological zones. India has much more to offer in terms of diversity in fruits. The country can boast of as many as 50 indigenous fruits. And if you take their allied species and wild relatives into account, the number of native varieties goes up to 400. The types of fruits found in diverse atmospheric conditions are divided into different agroecological regions (Table-1). Overall, around 20-25 vegetable crops hold commercial importance, encompassing both indigenous and exotic species with considerable variability. A wide range of vegetable crops is cultivated throughout the country owing to availability of suitable agro- climatic conditions. Temperate vegetables, however, require more specific growing conditions and are predominantly cultivated in the Himalayan region, with limited production occurring at higher elevations of the Western and Eastern Ghats. The diversity of vegetable crops, including both cultivated and wild species, is widespread across India. Ecosystem diversity: At the ecosystem level, India demonstrates remarkable diversity, encompassing deserts, rainforests, mangroves, coral reefs, wetlands, estuaries, and alpine meadows, thereby reflecting an exceptionally rich range of ecosystems. It measures the wide diversity of communities which includes grasslands, fields, lakes and forests. Ecosystem diversity encompasses both genetic and species variation, earning recognition as the “largest scale of biodiversity.” The benefits derived from this diversity such as nutrient cycling, carbon storage, pest regulation, and pollination are indispensable for sustaining agricultural productivity. Ensuring the healthy operational of ecosystems not only strengthens the plasticity of agriculture as it intensifies to meet rising food demands, but also safeguards the ecological processes upon which human survival, livelihoods, and long-term well-being depend. In horticultural systems, biodiversity at ecosystem level includes orchards, polyhouses, mixed cropping systems. Orchard is a place where a number of fruit crops have been planted in systemic manner and are overseen to produce profits through consecutive yields. Protected cultivation encompasses techniques such as polyhouses, mulch use, direct covers, windbreaks, and tunnel-based greenhouses. Among these, polyhouses offer a highly controlled growing environment by regulating temperature, solar exposure, airflow and humidity. This technological innovation has transformed conventional farming, making it more resource-efficient and productive. Rising consumer demand for off-season produce has further enhanced the relevance of polyhouse farming.
Ecosystem services can provide following benefits:
Provisioning services: Supply essentials such as food, fresh water, fuelwood, fiber, biochemicals, and genetic resources.
Regulating services: Maintain balance through climate regulation, disease control, water regulation and purification, and pollination.
Supporting services: Provide foundational processes like soil formation, nutrient cycling, and primary production that sustain ecosystems.
Cultural services: Enrich human life through spiritual and religious values, recreation, ecotourism, aesthetic inspiration, education, cultural heritage, and sense of place.
BENEFITS OF BIODIVERSITY:

Humans derive untold direct economic benefits from nature, including food resources such as fruits, cereals, and pulses; fibers and construction materials; industrial products like tannins, dyes, resins, and lubricants; as well as a wide array of medicinally important substances. These natural provisions not only sustain daily life but also form the foundation of health, industry, and livelihoods, underscoring humanity’s deep dependence on biodiversity. Biodiversity supports ecosystem services including air quality, climate, water purification, pollination and prevention of erosion (Costanza et al., 1997). Non-material benefits including spiritual and aesthetic values, knowledge system and the value of erosion (Hassan et al., 2006). Human societies have already gained immense direct economic advantages from biodiversity, drawing upon it for essential resources such as food, clothing, and medicine. These contributions from nature not only sustain daily life but also form the foundation of health, livelihoods, and cultural development, underscoring humanity’s profound dependence on biological wealth. A diverse garden or orchard resists pests better, thrives under climate stress, and reduces reliance on chemical fertilizers and pesticides. Environmental benefits of horticulture can be highlighted through the assessment of greenhouse gas emissions from the production of ornamental plants. It indicates that even in the windy season, or high temperature season these help in maintaining the ambient atmosphere for the plant growth. The benefits of biodiversity are summarised below:
Preserving Rare Plant Species:

The numerous animal species and plant which are vulnerable and endangered live in the ecosystem biodiversity which are currently hunted by man for their personal treasures. Across vast expense of the country, from the Western Ghats to the Eastern Himalayas, Horticultural practices have been utilized to cultivate and thereby conserve numerous plant species that face threats in their natural habitats. Botanical gardens, national parks, seed banks and gene banks are methods for conservation of biodiversity. Cryopreservation, a long-term ex-situ method involves storing of plant tissues, cells and its parts or organ in liquid nitrogen at -196 degree Celsius. Also, the various research institutions, and Private collectors also contribute to the conservation of threatened species by maintaining them in controlled conditions that promote their flourishing. The propagation of rare plants can lead to rehabilitation of habitats, contributing to the restoration of degraded ecosystems. The preservation also helps in the diversification of indigenous plant species which can bloom in that area at its full potential.
Landscaping Practices and Wildlife Habitats:

The use of diverse plant species in landscaping significantly contributes to the enhancement of urban biodiversity. In India, where the floral diversity is vast, horticultural practices that emphasize the use of a variety of indigenous plants can create habitats that are rich in biodiversity. Native plants are particularly important as they have evolved in concert with the local fauna and thus are more likely to provide the appropriate food and habitat for local insect and bird species. The inclusion of flowering plants, shrubs, and trees that provide nectar, pollen, fruits, and seeds, as well as nesting and hiding places, Such landscapes can attract a wide variety of birds, butterflies, bees, and other beneficial insects, thereby enriching urban biodiversity and strengthening ecological interactions that support both nature and human well-being. These organisms, in turn, contribute to the pollination of plants, control of pest populations, and overall health of the urban ecosystem. Horticulture offers green spaces in the urban areas through rooftop garden, urban parks and vertical gardens which not only provides greenery but develops small ecosystem for birds, insects and small mammals offering them food, shelter and breeding sites. Also, it provides movement of wildlife in these urban corridors which is decreasing as a result of the growing pollution and climate change. The dwelling species require particular environment for their activity hence; establishment of small orchards can help them to survive and also prevent them from migrating from that particular area
Sustainable Horticultural Practices with Technological Advancements:

Sustainable horticulture emphasizes the reduction of inputs like synthetic pesticides, fertilizers and fungicides, the conservation of water, the maintenance of genetic heterogeneity and the improvement of soil health. By adopting an integrated approach, horticultural practices not only aid in conserving biodiversity but also strengthen agricultural productivity and resilience against climate change, diseases, and pests. In India, the advancement of sustainable horticulture is driven by a synergy of traditional knowledge and modern scientific innovations, fostering techniques that are environmentally responsible, economically sustainable, and socially inclusive. This balance ensures that agriculture continues to thrive while safeguarding ecological integrity and supporting community well-being. The adoption of developing technologies in India has taken a leading role to support sustainable horticulture. The important development is precision agriculture are tools like GPS, drones, and IoT based sensors. These technologies help optimize the use of water, nutrients, and pest control methods, thereby reducing environmental impact. They also allow farmers to monitor and manage crops more accurately, minimizing waste and environmental impact. Furthermore, hydroponics and other soilless cultivation methods are becoming increasingly popular, especially in urban settings. These systems use nutrient rich water which contains optimum nutrient for plant growth and development without the need for soil.
THREATS FOR BIODIVERSITY:

The biological wealth is facing issues day by day and hence it is recording a significant decrease and the main role played here is by humans and their activities. The human encroachment upon wild areas like deforestation and the expansion of road networks have emerged as pressing environmental concerns. The destruction of habitats, along with the proliferation of invasive exotic species has significantly contributed to species extinction, particularly in tropical rainforest regions. In general, biodiversity loss within a region can result in reduced plant productivity, diminished resilience to adverse environmental conditions such as floods and droughts, and greater fluctuations in key ecosystem processes, including plant growth, water utilization, and the cycles of pests and diseases. Such disruptions not only weaken ecological stability but also threaten agricultural sustainability and human livelihoods that depend on these natural systems. The “Evil Quartet” is a term coined by ecologist Jared Diamond to describe the four major, human driven forces of biodiversity loss and species extinction.

These factors are a) Habitat degradation and fragmentation b) Unsustainable exploitation of natural resources c) Invasion by non-native (alien) species d) Co-extinction resulting from the loss of interdependent species. Endemic species are especially vulnerable and may face extinction due to uncontrolled hybridization, genetic mixing and genetic swamping. Additionally, genetically modified crops have emerged serving as a source of genetic contamination.
CONSERVATION APPROACHES AND METHODS:

The maintenance of horticultural crops is primarily unorganised. Complementary strategies can be employed together in in-situ and ex-situ conservation within essential crop groups is achieved through two complementary approaches: in-situ conservation, which involves protecting species within their natural habitats, and ex-situ conservation, which ensures their preservation outside of these native environments.
Ex-situ Conservation:

The preservation of germplasm outside its natural habitat is termed ex-situ conservation. Germplasm can be conserved by seedlings, pollen, clonal material, seed and DNA. It is essential for the system to also be set up to achieve that reproductive materials are readily available, either through a gene bank or from a production source situated in the area where they will be used.
Field gene bank:

Field gene bank conservation involves collecting plant materials from farms, gardens, or natural habitats and relocating it to a different site where it can be cultivated and observed. In field gene banks, plant genetic resources are conserved as living collections that continue to grow and therefore demand ongoing care and management. Designed primarily for ex-situ conservation, field gene banks maintain individual plants through horticultural practices, making them particularly valuable for species that produce recalcitrant seeds or are propagated vegetatively, especially those of agricultural significance. For crops with extended juvenile phases, such as many fruit trees, field gene banks provide rapid and convenient access to conserved material for research and utilization. Moreover, for several species, alternative conservation methods remain insufficiently developed for effective application. The ex-situ maintenance of tree species through field gene banks requires the preservation of a extensive range of genotypes to ensure genetic diversity, which in turn necessitates extensive land resources particularly for large tree species and involves considerable maintenance costs. As a complementary strategy, vegetatively propagated plants can also be safeguarded in clonal repositories, offering an alternative means of conservation.
b) Seed gene bank:

A seed bank is an area where different crop species are conserved or preserved outside their natural home; therefore, it comes under general kind of ex situ type of conservation. Seed banks have special facilities that conserve the seed according to their required temperature. These processes help maintain the viability of different kinds of stored seeds and provide material for future research purpose. It has been reported that the conservation of domesticated crop species in seed bank has been practiced since ancient times.

Seed banks act as vital repositories where a wide range of crop species are safeguarded beyond their natural habitats, representing a key form of ex-situ conservation. Equipped with specialized facilities that regulate temperature, they ensure the continued viability of stored seeds. This preservation not only secures genetic diversity for the long term but also serves as a valuable resource for future research and crop improvement. The practice of storing domesticated crop species in seed banks is deeply rooted in history, with evidence indicating that such various conservation measures have been undertaken. since ancient times, reflecting humanity’s enduring reliance on biodiversity for survival and progress. This approach is widely used for storing orthodox seeds, especially those of vegetable crops. Since seeds can remain viable for long periods when kept under ideal storage conditions, frequent regeneration is not required. As a result, reducing the need for regular regeneration helps in maintaining germplasm more economically. It also helps to minimize genetic erosion caused by genetic drift in small populations that are cultivated for regeneration. Collections are maintained in two forms. (i) active collections, which are stored under medium- term conditions (around 4°C) and are used for evaluation and distribution of samples and (ii) base collections are preserved at about -20°C for long- term storage. Additionally, research is ongoing to develop alternative seed storage techniques (recalcitrant seed storage for high moisture), cryopreservation of seeds and storage of ultra dry seeds.
c) In vitro conservation:

Certain crop plants like banana and plantain (Musa spp.) either exhibit an absence of seed production or synthesize recalcitrant seeds, similar to crops including coconut, cocoa and many trees and shrubs. Crops like cassava, potato, yam and sweet potato often have genetically sterile lines or produce orthodox seeds that are highly heterozygous. As a result, seed storage is not very useful for preserving specific genetic combinations. These crops are generally propagated vegetatively to preserve their genetic integrity, resulting in clones with an identical genetic makeup. Currently, the most prevalent method of conserving the genetic resources of such crops is by maintaining whole plants in the field. However, field gene banks face several challenges. The distribution and dissemination of plant material from these gene banks are difficult due to their vegetative nature and the higher risk of disease transmission. Additionally, conserving the preservation of rare and endangered plant species has become important concern. To overcome these limitations, plant tissue culture repositories and cryopreservation methods are used for conserving genetic resources. Tissue culture techniques serve a critical function in the collection, multiplication, and preservation of plant germplasm, as they enable efficient and large-scale propagation of plant material. Furthermore, virus-free plants can be generated through the application of the integration of meristem culture and thermotherapy, ensuring healthier and more reliable genetic resources for retention and crop improvement. Which helps in obtaining disease- free planting material and makes quarantine procedures easier. The use of small- sized explants reduces the space required for storage and also lowers labour costs.

At the in vitro repository of NBPGR, New Delhi, several horticultural crop germplasms are conserved, including vegetables (29054), fruits and nuts (302), medicinal and aromatic plants (9530) and ornamental plants (743) accessions respectively.
d) Cryopreservation:

Cryopreservation involves the storage of plant material at ultra-low temperatures, most often carried out using liquid nitrogen or its vapor (ranging from about -154°C to -196°C). In this environment, cell division and metabolic activities come to complete halt, allowing plant materials to be retained for extended periods without any changes. This approach is highly suitable for regeneration of whole plants from stored propagules which provides long term conservation of germplasm. At the cryobank of NBPGR, New Delhi, cryopreserved horticultural germplasm includes 207 accessions as per its annual report 2024. Cryopreservation requires minimal storage space, involves low maintenance, and is considered a cost- effective conservation method.
e) Pollen storage:

Pollen storage was primarily developed to facilitate controlled pollination among genotypes that flower at different times, particularly in fruit tree species. This technique affords several significant benefits for germplasm conservation, as only a small quantity of pollen is required for each accession. The dissemination of germplasm via pollen is subject to fewer quarantine restrictions compared to seeds or other planting materials. In the past few years, cryopreservation techniques have evolved to increasingly applied to pollen from a diverse range of species, leading to the establishment of pollen cryobanks for fruit trees in several countries. However, the retention of pollen alone is insufficient to reflect the complete diversity of cytoplasmic genomes within a species. Therefore, it is important to evaluate the limitations of apart from maternal contributions genetic components and to explore alternatives such as preservation of ovules together with in vitro fertilization techniques. Additionally, efficient sampling strategies are necessary to adequately represent the genetic diversity of populations or gene pools.
f) Botanical and herbal gardens:

Botanical gardens play a key role in conserving biodiversity by serving as safe havens for endangered species, offering living ecological models, and nurturing both genetic and species diversity. Beyond their scientific function, they also strengthen global collaboration in safeguarding plant germplasm, while fostering public awareness and appreciation of the natural world. In this way, botanical gardens bridge conservation with education and cultural values, highlighting the enduring relationship among human societies and plant diversity. Botanical gardens generally have a limited role in preserving the genetic variability of species because they maintain a limited number of accessions for each species or taxonomic group. Nevertheless, they contribute significantly to public awareness and education. These gardens are primarily used to exhibit a wide range of exotic plant species. In some well- managed cases, they may also focus on conserving specific groups of plants as living collections. Botanical gardens can play a very important role in agricultural studies. Further botanical gardens help in greening of cities, developing tourist destinations and also commercial enterprises. Herbal gardens are similar to botanical gardens but specifically focus on conservation of medicinal and aromatic plants. Their importance has increased in recent years, as these plant groups are among the most threatened within horticultural species.
In- situ conservation:

In-situ conservation entails safeguarding plant species within their indigenous range habitats, thereby allowing natural evolutionary processes to proceed and sustaining a dynamic ecological system. Genetic diversity arises through mutation, the spread of pollen and seeds, and recombination within and between populations. Natural selection acts on this diversity, enabling the development of more resilient plant varieties that are adapted. Besides conserving plants in legally protected areas and national parks, In-situ conservation also encompasses on-farm practices, where traditional crop varieties and indigenous landraces are cultivated and maintained. This approach depends on the active involvement of farmers to preserve these traditional varieties. Genetic resources can even be maintained in domestic gardens. The practice of on-farm conservation is especially important in regions such as India, as it helps preserve area-specific genetic diversity and supports the production of a broad array of food and related products for households and local markets. This approach is particularly crucial in regions where livelihoods depend on traditional subsistence farming. A range of on-farm conservation strategies has been proposed to identify which crop varieties should be preserved and in which locations, with due consideration of both biological considerations and socio-economic factors.
Innovations in Horticultural conservation:

The combination of modern technology, traditional knowledge, and advanced breeding methods has led to a new phase in conservation horticulture in India, endowed with rich biodiversity and strong agricultural heritage. These innovations not only increase productivity and sustainability but also serve a pivotal function in preserving biodiversity, which is increasingly important in the response to climate change and rising food security challenges.
Technological advancements in Sustainable Horticulture:

India has been a leader in adopting and developing technologies that uphold sustainable horticultural practices. For example, precision agriculture has gained wider adoption, using tools such as GPS, drones, and IoT-based sensors to efficiently manage water usage, nutrient supply, and pest control. This approach minimizes the environmental effects of agricultural activities while enabling farmers to monitor and manage crops with a high degree of precision, cutting down waste and ensuring plants receive optimal inputs for growth. Additionally, hydroponics and other soil-free farming approaches are becoming increasingly popular, especially in cities where land is scarce. These techniques rely on nutrient-rich water solutions to grow plants, lowering water consumption, removing the need for soil, and reducing the likelihood of soil-related diseases. They can be implemented on rooftops or in unused urban areas, helping to enhance urban biodiversity while supplying fresh produce locally and decreasing transportation distances.
Breeding Programs for Resilience and Diversity:

India, recognizing the indispensable role of genetic diversity in sustaining agriculture, has invested in breeding programs designed to develop crop varieties resilient to pests, diseases, and the growing challenges of climate change. These initiatives frequently integrate traditional cultivars and wild relatives, weaving together centuries of indigenous knowledge with modern science. By adopting this approach, they not only ensure food security but also honor the cultural heritage embedded in farming practices, reflecting a close association between humans survival and the preservation of biodiversity. which possess valuable traits. The goal is to produce genetically diverse crops capable of adapting to different environmental stresses, thereby strengthening food security and improving the resilience of farming systems. For instance, the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) has been instrumental in creating and promoting climate-resilient crops, including drought-tolerant varieties of rice, wheat, and millet. These efforts not only contribute to sustainable food production but also help conserve the genetic resources required to sustain future crop improvement initiatives
Global and Local initiatives for biodiversity conservation of horticulture:

India is actively participating in both international and domestic efforts to promote biodiversity conservation through horticulture. On the global stage, India, as a signatory in accordance with the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), has pledged to meet the Aichi Biodiversity Targets, which emphasize sustainable agriculture and the safeguarding of genetic diversity. Nationwide, initiatives such as the National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture (NMSA) and the National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) integrate biodiversity conservation into farming practices, ensuring that agricultural development is aligned with ecological sustainability and long-term resilience. At the grassroots level, many NGOs and community-based groups are working to preserve traditional horticultural knowledge and methods that support biodiversity. Initiatives like Navdanya have formed the foundation for conserving heirloom seeds and encouraging organic farming, helping to protect agricultural biodiversity. Additionally, government efforts to promote organic farming-illustrated by states like Sikkim’s transition to fully organic farming reflects a strong commitment to enhancing soil health, reducing dependence on chemical inputs, and sustaining ecological balance. This approach not only safeguards the environment but also supports the livelihoods of farming communities by promoting sustainable agricultural practices rooted in harmony with nature. Altogether, these initiatives not only safeguard biodiversity but also support sustainable livelihoods for farmers and local communities.
